cases.interviewerQuestion: Bearer-token auth had to stand in for cookies since the extension lives outside the main app's domain — what did that tradeoff cost you in terms of session management or security compared to the cookie-based flow the core app uses?
cases.tonyRaw: Nothing in what I searched applies to this specific integration, so I'll answer from what I actually own here. The real cost of bearer tokens over cookies was that I had to take on session lifecycle management explicitly instead of getting it for free from the browser — token issuance, expiry, and refresh all became my responsibility on the extension's API layer rather than something the core app's cookie infrastructure handled implicitly. It also meant being more deliberate about where the token lived in the extension's storage and making sure every one of those 30-plus route handlers validated it consistently, since there was no shared domain boundary doing that enforcement for me. I don't want to overstate the security delta without pulling up the actual implementation details, but functionally it shifted trust from "the browser enforces same-origin" to "the API layer has to correctly enforce it on every request," which is a heavier and more error-prone guarantee to hold.

cases.interviewerQuestion: Before you landed on three distinct layers, what did the undifferentiated store actually look like, and what was the specific bug that made it clear real-time, server, and local UI state couldn't keep living together?
cases.tonyRaw: Before the split, everything lived in one shared store — Liveblocks presence and cursor data, server-fetched document state, and local UI state like modal or panel toggles were all sitting in the same context, so a change in any one of them triggered re-renders and reconciliation across the others. The bug that made it undeniable was a TanStack Query cache invalidation clobbering in-flight collaborative state: because server refetches and Liveblocks updates weren't isolated from each other, a stale server response could overwrite state a user was actively editing in real time, so their change would silently revert. That's not a bug you patch around — the three domains have genuinely different update cadences and consistency guarantees — so I split them into Liveblocks typed LiveObject/LiveList for real-time state, TanStack Query with proper cache invalidation boundaries for server state, and a Context/reducer layer for local UI state, and I owned all three of those pieces solo.

cases.interviewerQuestion: Supporting two concurrent editor versions while integrating AI output into ProseMirror's typed node model sounds like it could double the surface area for bugs. What was the hardest part of keeping that state-management layer consistent across both versions?
cases.tonyRaw: I co-led the team of 3 to 4 engineers on that project, and I personally designed the state-management layer, so this part fell squarely on me. The hardest part wasn't the AI integration itself, it was that the two editor versions had diverging assumptions about the document model, and any AI-generated content had to resolve into a valid typed node structure in both without the state layer knowing which version it was talking to. So I designed the integration point to normalize AI output into a shape that respected the typed node contract generically, rather than writing version-specific branches, which kept the surface area from actually doubling. The real discipline was resisting the urge to special-case the older version every time something didn't fit cleanly.

cases.interviewerQuestion: Since Spanner and Cloud Dataflow were both brand new to the team, how did you validate that the staged migrations and regression tests would actually catch problems in a system nobody on the team had production experience with yet?
cases.tonyRaw: I co-led our SQL to Google Cloud Spanner migration, learning Spanner and Cloud Dataflow alongside the rest of the team as we drove a $500K per year infrastructure cost reduction, and the newness of both tools is exactly why we leaned so hard on staging things in small, reversible pieces rather than trusting our judgment about what "should" work. We ran migrations in phases with report-only passes first — comparing row counts, checksums, and query results against the legacy SQL system before ever cutting over — so a mistake surfaced as a diff we could inspect, not a production incident. Regression tests were built against known-good outputs from the old system, so instead of needing deep Spanner expertise to know what correct looked like, we just needed the two systems to agree, which sidesteps the inexperience problem rather than pretending it away. Where we did hit gaps in our Dataflow assumptions, the staged rollout meant we caught them at the report stage, before any data actually moved.

cases.interviewerQuestion: What was actually breaking on long meetings before the chunking work — was it the model losing earlier context, hitting hard token limits, or something else — and how did that shape the way you decided to split transcripts into chunks?
cases.tonyRaw: The core issue wasn't the model losing earlier context mid-conversation — it was that a long meeting transcript plus everything else Smith needed in context would blow past the token budget before the model ever got to reason about it, so you'd hit a hard limit rather than a gradual degradation. That shaped the chunking decision: instead of just truncating or summarizing blindly, I split transcripts in a way that preserved enough continuity across chunks that tool-selection and artifact decisions downstream still had the context they needed, rather than each chunk being processed in isolation and losing the thread of the meeting. I contributed to an existing agentic assistant rather than architecting it from scratch — my specific ownership was that transcript-chunking and context-window handling, plus the tool-selection prompting improvements that depended on the chunks being coherent. Getting the chunk boundaries right mattered more than raw size, since a bad split could hand the model a chunk that made no sense without the one before it.

cases.interviewerQuestion: You emphasize that the computation was already server-side and the real work was the architectural port itself — what made validating calculation accuracy for high-volume trader accounts tricky enough to require close stakeholder involvement?
cases.tonyRaw: I worked on porting our trade metric computation from a TypeORM-based implementation into our new GraphQL API architecture, validating calculation accuracy with stakeholders along the way. The tricky part wasn't the math itself, it was making sure the port didn't silently change behavior at the edges — high-volume trader accounts accumulate a lot of trade history, and small differences in how the old TypeORM queries aggregated or ordered records versus the new GraphQL resolvers could produce numbers that were close but not identical. Those discrepancies only show up when you're looking at accounts with real volume, so I needed stakeholders who knew what the "correct" figures should look like to sanity-check outputs against the legacy system rather than just trusting that a clean port meant a correct one. That back-and-forth was really about building confidence in equivalence, not debugging a broken calculation.

cases.interviewerQuestion: You spent nine months iterating on the delay and timing for the debounced autosave. What made that tuning so hard to nail down — what kept pulling you back to adjust it?
cases.tonyRaw: I want to push back a little on "nine months of continuous tuning" — I built the original debounced autosave and iterated on the delay and dirty-state tracking over that period, but it wasn't a constant grind on one number the whole time. It came up whenever usage patterns exposed a new edge case: too short a delay and you're firing saves on every keystroke pause, too long and users feel like their work isn't safe, and the dirty-state tracking had to be right so we weren't saving no-op states. So the adjustments were episodic, driven by real editing behavior in the artifact editor, not a single nine-month tuning session. After I rotated off to the next engagement, a teammate reworked the editor-specific hook further to fix stale-closure and grace-period issues, but that refinement was their work, not mine.

cases.interviewerQuestion: Before you write code, how do you decide whether a decision needs to be written down first?

cases.interviewerQuestion: Have you had a check you wrote keep failing in new ways? What did you change in the end?
cases.tonyRaw: This is actually the persona-safety check behind me, not a Topstep story, but it's the clearest example I have of a check that kept failing in new ways. I built the guard that stops this persona from ever claiming a current OT licence, and for eight rounds I kept hardening the pattern matcher — tightening word boundaries, extending enumerations — and every fix just introduced a new bypass or blind spot in the next round. The real problem, laid out in my spec on the second layer, was that assert-versus-deny isn't a property you can catch with character patterns; the pattern matcher literally couldn't represent the distinction it was being asked to make. So I stopped trying to make regex smarter and added a second layer instead: one cheap model call that reads the sentence and answers yes-or-no, running only when the topic comes up, and set it to fail closed so an uncertain case gets a scripted safe reply instead of an unverified one.
